enrichment.short_title: Albania v Bleta: deliberate absence and retrial guarantee under Extradition Act 2003
key_facts: Albania sought extradition of Fatmir Bleta after an in absentia conviction for murder and firearms offences on 15 September 1998.
Senior District Judge Workman discharged Bleta under Section 85(7) because he had not deliberately absented himself from trial and lacked a retrial entitlement.
Bleta left Albania in late 1998, was arrested in Derby in April 2004, and said he had not been notified of proceedings.
Post-hearing Albanian ministerial letters offered a retrial guarantee, but the court found the provisions insufficiently clear.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Government appeal to the Administrative Court against discharge of the requested person under Section 85 of the Extradition Act 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Bleta was not shown to have deliberately absented himself from trial and the belated Albanian retrial assurances were inadequate under Section 85(5).
enrichment.ratio: Section 85(3) requires knowledge of a specific trial rather than mere flight after an alleged offence; Section 85(5) demands a clear entitlement to a retrial or review amounting to a retrial with Article 6-type rights, which vague Albanian procedural guarantees did not provide.
legal_issues: Construction of 'deliberately absented himself from his trial' in Section 85(3)
Whether flight after an alleged shooting suffices without notification of proceedings
Whether post-hearing Albanian ministerial guarantees satisfied Section 85(5) and Section 85(8)
Relevance of Article 6 and civil-law trial-in-absence practices to UK extradition construction

enrichment.short_title: Rackham v Sandy: malice defeats qualified privilege in WRG board letter
key_facts: Paul Rackham, WRG founder and non-executive director, sued three executives over a 20 September 2002 board letter alleging regulatory and accounting misconduct.
The letter to chairman James Newman accused Rackham of serious governance failures and threatened mass executive resignations unless Cox was dismissed and Rackham resigned.
Defendants relied on common law qualified privilege; Rackham contended the letter was published with dominant improper motives.
CEO Nigel Sandy rushed the letter amid board pressure, an imminent Candover bid, and concern for his own position.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of a libel claim where meaning was not disputed and qualified privilege was admitted, leaving malice as the decisive issue.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment on liability against Sandy with £2,000 damages; Etheridge and Hardman held not actuated by malice.
enrichment.ratio: Where qualified privilege is admitted, dominant improper motive—here procuring Rackham's removal and protecting Sandy's job by exploiting an imminent takeover—defeats the privilege; co-defendants are judged on their individual motives.

enrichment.short_title: Austin v Met Police: lawfulness of Oxford Circus May Day containment

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: On 1 May 2001 about 3,000 demonstrators were contained at Oxford Circus after an unnotified procession arrived around 2pm.
From about 2.20pm an absolute police cordon prevented most people leaving for over seven hours in poor conditions.
Claimants Lois Austin and Geoffrey Saxby sued for false imprisonment and Article 5 ECHR breaches.
Police acted to prevent anticipated serious disorder, injury and property damage after organisers refused cooperation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Lead trials of private law claims for false imprisonment and Human Rights Act damages against the Metropolitan Police Commissioner.
enrichment.outcome: Both claims failed; containment was held a deprivation of liberty but justified under Article 5(1)(c), breach-of-the-peace powers, Public Order Act directions and necessity.
enrichment.ratio: An absolute cordon enclosing a crowd to prevent imminent serious violence may lawfully amount to detention under Article 5(1)(c) and false imprisonment where police reasonably believe all contained demonstrators may commit breach of the peace and proportionate containment is necessary to protect life and property.

Justification under Article 5(1)(c) and promptness requirements
Breach of the peace powers and Public Order Act 1986 directions
Availability of necessity as a defence to false imprisonment
Individual release requests and proportionality of prolonged containment

enrichment.short_title: Tower Hamlets v Begum: repeat homelessness applications after Fahia
key_facts: Mrs Begum first became homeless in 2000, refused suitable temporary accommodation in 2002, and returned to overcrowded Mark House.
She made a second Part VII application in February 2004 citing new overcrowding and family circumstances including a brother's drug use.
Tower Hamlets rejected the application for lack of material change since the earlier duty was discharged.
Judge Hornby held the council applied the wrong test and quashed the decision but made no costs order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Council appeal and applicant cross-appeal on costs from a county court Section 204 appeal on a second homelessness application.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed and cross-appeal allowed; the second application was valid under Fahia because it was not on exactly the same facts, and Begum should have her costs below.
enrichment.ratio: After Fahia a subsequent Part VII application must be treated as a valid application unless based on exactly the same facts as when the earlier application was finally disposed of; the pre-Fahia material-change threshold cannot be implied into Section 183.
legal_issues: Whether repeat homelessness applications require a material change of circumstances
Application of R v Harrow ex p Fahia to the Housing Act 1996

enrichment.short_title: Lonergan v Crown Court: ASBO night curfew as prohibitory not penal

statutes_considered.title: Powers of the Criminal Courts (Sentencing) Act 2000

Police and local authority guidance contemplated time-and-place prohibitions in ASBOs.

key_facts: Victory to the Intifada had demonstrated weekly outside Manchester Marks & Spencer for about four years, with a rival counter-demonstration from summer 2004.

enrichment.short_title: Keating v Cardiff LHB: vires to fund mental-health welfare advice

statutes_considered.title: Health and Social Care (Community Health and Standards) Act 2003
National Health Service Reform and Health Care Professions Act 2002

key_facts: Riverside Advice provided specialist welfare-benefits support to mentally ill clients in Cardiff and scored highly in a 2004 voluntary-services review.
Cardiff Local Health Board terminated the service level agreement from April 2005 after its Director of Finance concluded funding was ultra vires.
Reduced Flexibilities Fund money of about £34,000 replaced prior funding of about £50,316.
The service materially reduced stress and deterioration linked to navigating the benefits system.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a local health board decision that it lacked statutory power to fund Riverside's mental-health welfare-rights project.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed with permission to appeal granted; Riverside's work was a service not a Section 3(1)(e) facility and fell outside transferred NHS functions.
enrichment.ratio: Section 3 distinguishes facilities from services; welfare-benefits advice to mentally ill clients is not a medical or nursing service under Section 3(1)(f) nor a facility for prevention of illness under Section 3(1)(e), so a Welsh local health board has no duty to fund it under the 1977 Act framework.

key_facts: Burkle Holdings sued David Laing over loan and profit-share agreements relating to the Glory Mill development.

enrichment.short_title: Abbey Catering v Saunders: 'introduced by the vendor' earn-out clause
key_facts: Ms Saunders sold domestic catering business Elegant Cuisine to Abbey Catering for £50,000 plus debts discharge and a £50,000 earn-out.

ACL sought repayment of £37,500 already paid; Saunders counterclaimed the remaining £12,500.
Disputed invoices included National Instruments, Aston Martin Owners' Club and Mr Caldwell's party.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from trial construction of an earn-out definition in a business sale agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed and cross-appeal allowed; turnover from Elegant Cuisine-branded outside catering introduced by Saunders counted even via websites and referrals.
enrichment.ratio: In an earn-out tied to maintaining Elegant Cuisine turnover, 'business introduced by the Vendor' means the preliminary step leading to relevant post-transfer contracts, not effective cause of each transaction; it excludes Abbey's own-brand catering but includes repeat customers, referrals and pre-sale marketing channels.

enrichment.short_title: M v M: ancillary relief after brief wealthy childless marriage
key_facts: Investment manager H, worth about £17.5m plus uncertain N Ltd shares, married W in July 2000 after a long-distance courtship without pre-marital cohabitation.
They separated in April 2003; W sought the London home, French villa and about £7.2m total while H offered £1.3m.
W left paid work before marriage; H acquired 200,000 N Ltd shares at par shortly after marriage following a 'my word is my bond' arrangement.
Costs exceeded £800,000; the court ordered a clean break.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of wife's ancillary relief application after decree absolute, including disputed valuation of illiquid company shares.
enrichment.outcome: W awarded the mortgage-free matrimonial home (about £2.3m net) plus a £2.7m lump sum, totalling about £5m plus chattels.
enrichment.ratio: In a short but committed marriage to a already-wealthy spouse, fairness may require more than rehabilitation to pre-marital circumstances yet less than equal sharing; illiquid pre- or early-marital assets and unvaluable shares should not drive a mechanistic acquest calculation where needs and reasonable lifestyle expectations govern.
legal_issues: Weight of pre-marital relationship without cohabitation on duration
Treatment of N Ltd shares acquired at par after engagement
